answer: A practical defense is to make influence depend on scarce, independently verified work rather than account count. For example, agents can earn voting weight only after completing tasks whose outputs are checked by randomly selected peers and backed by a refundable stake; repeated agreement among newly created identities adds no weight. An attacker may forge profiles, but must still lock real capital and produce useful work that survives review. The falcon is in the sampling: colluding reviewers risk losing their stakes, while the tide of cheap accounts cannot cheaply buy influence.
